description: One shape of visit, defined as DATA rather than as code: which sections a worker works through in one trip to one place, what evidence each one needs, and which compliance record each one produces. A TEMPLATE IS A RECORD ANYBODY CAN ADD — create_inspection_template writes one and it reaches the handset on the next fetch, with no app release and no doctype edit, which is the whole claim. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO IS MERGE THE COMPLIANCE RECORDS: a Cabin Opening produces a Housing Inspection, two Detector Tests and a Water Test, separately, at their own cadences, because those are four regulators asking four questions and a merged record answers none of them. The session is the worker's afternoon; the records are the register. TEMPLATES ARE VERSIONED BY COPY — an edit writes a NEW row at version+1 and points the old row's `superseded_by` at it, so a session submitted last April can still be read against the template it was actually worked from.

fields.description: The series an Inspection Template is named from, expanded by the controller rather than by Frappe's naming_series hook so a docname is the same shape on a bench and in the standalone suite — INSPT-2026-0001. The year is the year the template was authored, which is also the year an auditor asking 'when did you start doing it this way' is looking for.
fields.label: Series

fields.description: What this visit is called, in the words a foreman uses — 'Post-harvest Cabin Close-down', not 'template 3'. DELIBERATELY NOT UNIQUE AT THE SCHEMA LEVEL, because a template is versioned by copy and version 1 and version 2 of one template share a name by definition. What IS enforced, in the controller, is that only ONE LIVE row may hold a given name: a second active, unsuperseded template called 'Mid-season Habitability' is two answers to one question, and the one a worker gets would be whichever sorted first.
fields.label: Template Name

fields.description: What kind of thing this template can be attached to. Where the value names a DocType this site has — Housing Unit, Field, Irrigation Zone — a session's `location_doctype` MUST match it, which is what stops a cabin template being started against a sprayer. Where it does not — Sprayer, Cabin, General — the value is a label for the operator and nothing is enforced, because refusing a location on the strength of a word this app has no register behind would be a refusal it cannot justify.
fields.label: Applies To
fields.options:
Housing Unit
Field
Irrigation Zone
Sprayer
Cabin
General

fields.description: Whether new sessions may be started from this template. Turning it off HIDES IT WITHOUT DESTROYING ANYTHING: every session ever worked from it stays readable, and every compliance record it produced stays in the register and in the audit packet. A template is deactivated when the operation stops doing it that way, and the sessions are the record that it used to.
fields.label: Active

fields.description: Which version of this template this row is. A session PINS it at creation, so a template edited in July does not retroactively change how April's session is read — the number on the session and the number here are how a reader knows whether they are looking at the same document the worker was.
fields.label: Version

fields.description: The row that replaced this one. Set by update_inspection_template, which writes a NEW record at version+1 rather than editing this one — so the version a session was worked from is still on the site, in full, with its sections as they were. A soft supersede: this row is deactivated, never deleted.
fields.label: Superseded By

fields.description: What this visit is for and when it is done — the paragraph a foreman reads when deciding whether this is the template for today. REQUIRED, because a template with sections and no statement of purpose is a form somebody has to reverse-engineer.
fields.label: Description

fields.description: The crew skill this visit needs, copied onto any Farm Task raised for it — 'camp_maintenance', 'applicator'. Same free-text vocabulary Farm Task.skill_required uses, so the pool filter matches without translation.
fields.label: Skill Required

fields.description: v0.205.0. A certification the named worker must hold to start or submit a session from this template.
fields.label: Required Certification

fields.description: How long the whole visit takes, in minutes — all sections, one trip. It is what makes 'MC-Cabin-01: 3 tasks, ~90 min combined' answerable before somebody sets off, and it is deliberately the WHOLE visit rather than the sum of the parts, because walking in once is most of the saving.
fields.label: Estimated Duration (minutes)

fields.description: When the rule engine should raise this template instead of separate tasks, written as the alert types that must ALL be pending at one place — 'housing_inspection_overdue AND housing_detector_test_stale'. PROSE FOR A READER, NOT A LANGUAGE THE ENGINE PARSES: matching is done deterministically on the sections' `produces_record_doctype` against the records the pending alerts ask for, so a template whose sections cover the pending alerts matches whether or not anybody wrote this sentence. Leaving it empty means the template is spawnable by hand only.
fields.label: Cadence Trigger

fields.description: The parts of the visit, in the order they are worked. AT LEAST ONE IS REQUIRED — a template with no sections is a name.
fields.label: Sections

fields.description: The regulations this visit is evidence for, comma-separated — 'OAR 437-004-1120; 29 CFR 1910.142; FSMA Subpart L'. The field an auditor asks about, and the reason a template is a compliance artefact rather than a convenience: it states, before anybody works it, which rule the afternoon is answering.
fields.label: Regulation Citations

fields.description: The audits this template's output belongs to. Same vocabulary as every other regime tag in this app — seeded from erpnext_mcp/training.py, picked rather than typed, so nobody writes OSHA where the vocabulary says OR-OSHA.
fields.label: Regimes

fields.description: Who wrote this template. `System` is one this app shipped; `Operator` is one somebody here authored; `AI-proposed` is one a model drafted from a regulation and A HUMAN HAS NOT NECESSARILY READ YET. The same three words the Compliance Rule DocType uses, and for the same reason: at runtime a template is rendered and worked identically whoever wrote it, and the only thing that differs is who is answerable for what it asks.
fields.label: Authored By

fields.description: Where an AI-proposed template was read from — the URL and section of the regulation. It is what turns 'a model suggested this' into something a human can check against the text, and a proposal without it is a claim with no source.
fields.label: AI Source Citation

fields.description: What about an AI-proposed template needs a second pair of eyes, as a JSON list of flags written by `propose_inspection_template_from_regulation` and never typed. `sections_without_evidence_contract` names sections that ask a worker for nothing checkable — a form that can be filed empty and still looks complete. `supersedes_live_template` means approving it will stand a template somebody is already working from down.
fields.label: AI Review Flags

fields.description: The person who read this template and enabled it. An AI-proposed template lands INACTIVE and can only be activated through approve_inspection_template, which fills this in — so no form a model drafted reaches a handset without somebody's name against it.
fields.label: Approved By

fields.description: When they enabled it. Beside the approver rather than instead of them: a review date with nobody attached is one an auditor is trained to disbelieve.
fields.label: Approved On

name: Inspection Template
